title: A bubble, a mirage (167–171)
hookLine: look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage, and the king of death won't see you
carry: real for a moment, never solid
tomorrow: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)
last: NO ONE CAN DO IT FOR YOU.

lines: A SOAP BUBBLE IN THE SUN.
WATER ON THE HIGHWAY THAT ISN'T.
cards: Blow a soap bubble on a sunny day and watch it. For a second or two it holds the whole world on its skin: the sky, the trees, your own stretched face, swirling in rainbow colors. It's real.
And then, with no sound at all, it's gone. Or drive a highway in summer heat toward the shimmering pool on the road that never gets any closer. Real shimmer, no water.
Chapter thirteen of the Dhammapada hands you those two sights as glasses to see through.

teach.h: ROUSE YOURSELF: THE KING'S SON BEGS.
teach.b: The chapter opens with a wake-up call, verse one sixty-eight: "Rouse thyself! do not be idle! Follow the law of virtue!"

The commentary says the Buddha spoke it when he first came home to his father's city and walked the streets with his alms bowl. His father, the king, was mortified to see his son begging, and hurried to stop him.
The Buddha answered that going for alms was the custom of his lineage, the lineage of Buddhas.
Then today's line, verse one seventy: "Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world."
In Pali, a bubble is pubbuḷa, and a mirage is marīcikā. Neither is nothing. A bubble really shimmers; a mirage really shines.
They just aren't solid or lasting. That's the way of looking the verse asks for: not that the world doesn't matter, but that nothing in it will hold still or hold your weight forever.

And its promise is plain: the king of death does not see the one who looks this way. Verse one seventy-one adds a picture: the world is like a glittering royal chariot; fools sink into it, the wise don't cling.
A Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, closes with a list of similes in the same spirit, among them a dream, a bubble, dew and lightning.
Two very different texts, one shared image.

how: Buddhists across many schools reflect on impermanence with images like the bubble, the mirage and the dream, often in chanting or in teachings given at funerals.

o: a symbol of the soul rising after death
proof that the world is only an illusion
a picture of the world: real, brief, never solid

games.q: match each image to what it teaches.
p: real for a moment, then gone

s: the verse says the world doesn't matter at all
a bubble really shimmers; the point is that nothing in the world is solid or lasting.
the Diamond Sutra uses a bubble among its images too
its closing verse includes a dream, a bubble, dew and lightning.
the commentary links verse 168 to the Buddha's first return home
his father was mortified to see him begging for alms in the streets.

games.q: you're the king. your son, now the Buddha, has come home and is walking your city's streets with a begging bowl. what do you do?
o: hurry out to stop him; a prince doesn't beg.
hide in the palace and pretend not to see.
join him with a bowl of your own.
games.why: the commentary says the king rushed to stop him. the Buddha answered that alms-round is the custom of the Buddhas' lineage, and spoke verse 168.

practice: If you can, look at something that shimmers, bubbles in a glass of sparkling water, light on a window, your reflection in a dark screen; if not, picture one soap bubble floating in front of you, and watch its colors move without trying to catch it.
Then close your eyes and watch your thoughts the same way: each one shimmering, real for a moment, then gone with no sound.

wordCard.voice: A bubble. Verse one seventy: look upon the world as a bubble, as a mirage: shining, real for a moment, never solid.

orig.note: Pali: a mirage — the shimmer of heat that looks like water; paired with pubbuḷa, a bubble, in verse 170.

carryVoice: Your line: real for a moment, never solid. A worry that feels huge is a bubble too. See you tomorrow.
